To determine the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that for any selection of \( n \) distinct integers from the set \(\{1, 2, \ldots, 200\}\), there exists a subset of these integers whose sum is divisible by 20, we need to consider the properties of sums modulo 20. 

First, note that the set \(\{1, 2, \ldots, 200\}\) contains 200 elements. We can use the pigeonhole principle to analyze the possible sums of subsets of these integers modulo 20. Specifically, we need to ensure that among any \( n \) integers, there is a subset whose sum is congruent to 0 modulo 20.

Consider the possible remainders when any integer in the set is divided by 20. These remainders can be any of the 20 values: \(0, 1, 2, \ldots, 19\). If we select \( n \) integers, we need to ensure that there is a subset of these integers whose sum is divisible by 20. This can be achieved by considering the sums of all possible subsets of the selected integers modulo 20.

By the pigeonhole principle, if we select 21 integers, there must be at least two subsets of these integers whose sums are congruent modulo 20. Let these two subsets be \( A \) and \( B \) with sums \( S_A \) and \( S_B \) respectively, where \( S_A \equiv S_B \pmod{20} \). The difference \( S_A - S_B \) is then divisible by 20, and the subset of integers corresponding to this difference will have a sum divisible by 20.

Therefore, the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that for any selection of \( n \) distinct integers from the set \(\{1, 2, \ldots, 200\}\), there exists a subset of these integers whose sum is divisible by 20 is \( n = 21 \).
